**Regularized adjusted plus-minus (RAPM) estimates how many points per 100
possessions a player adds to her team's margin, holding fixed the other nine
players on the court.** `wehoop` publishes two RAPM estimates for NCAA Division I
women's basketball, and they answer different questions. League-wide RAPM
(`load_ncaa_wbb_rapm()`) puts every Division I player on one scale.
Within-team RAPM (`load_ncaa_wbb_rapm_within_team()`) splits one team's
performance among its own players and cannot be compared across teams.

This article explains both, how they are built, how they are checked, and their
limits. It condenses the official model card in the
[ncaa-wbb-hoops-data repository](https://github.com/sportsdataverse/ncaa-wbb-hoops-data/blob/main/docs/models/rapm.md);
numbers quoted from that card are labelled as such. The last section shows how
to fit RAPM yourself on WNBA possessions with `wnba_rapm()`.

## What the model estimates

Plain plus-minus credits a player with her team's point margin while she is on
the court. That rewards a bench player who happens to share the floor with the
best starter. RAPM fixes this by estimating every player's effect at once, so
each player's number is her effect with her teammates and opponents accounted
for.

| | League-wide (`load_ncaa_wbb_rapm()`) | Within-team (`load_ncaa_wbb_rapm_within_team()`) |
|---|---|---|
| Question | How much does this player add, on a scale shared by all of Division I? | How is this team's performance divided among its players? |
| Fit | One ridge regression over every Division I possession in a season | One fit per team, on that team's possessions |
| Comparable across teams | Yes | No, by construction |
| Columns | `orapm`, `drapm`, `rapm_net`, `off_poss`, `def_poss`, `estimand` | `rapm_off`, `rapm_def`, `rapm_net`, `team_off_poss`, `num_players` |
| Coverage | 2011 onward | 2010 onward |

In the league-wide file `rapm_net` is offense plus defense, in points per 100
possessions, and a positive defensive value is good; the within-team file signs
defense the other way (see [below](#within-team-rapm)). The `estimand` column (`"league"`) is on every
league-wide row so the two estimates are never confused.

## Loading the ratings

```{r libraries}
library(wehoop)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r load}
rapm <- load_ncaa_wbb_rapm(seasons = 2026)

nrow(rapm)
count(rapm, estimand)
```

The top of the 2025-26 season among players with at least 800 possessions,
offense and defense combined (the floor the model card uses for its
leaderboard):

```{r leaders}
rapm |>
  filter(off_poss + def_poss >= 800) |>
  arrange(desc(rapm_net)) |>
  select(player, team, off_poss, orapm, drapm, rapm_net) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  head(15)
```

## Data: possessions, lineups and stints

RAPM needs to know who was on the court for every possession. The NCAA engine
reconstructs that from stats.ncaa.org play-by-play by tracking substitutions,
and `wehoop` publishes each layer:

- `load_ncaa_wbb_matchup_stints()`: one row per stretch of play with the same
  ten players on the court, with the score at its start and end.
- `load_ncaa_wbb_possessions()`: one row per possession, with both lineups and
  the points scored.
- `load_ncaa_wbb_lineups()`: lineup-level summaries.

```{r stints}
stints <- load_ncaa_wbb_matchup_stints(seasons = 2026)

nrow(stints)

stints |>
  select(home, away, period, duration_seconds, n_possessions,
         home_lineup, home_pts, away_pts) |>
  head(3)
```

As reported in the model card, the inputs are the published possessions, team
rosters and a name-change table that keeps a player in one column across
transfers and spelling variants. Seasons whose usable-possession share falls
below a gate are excluded; 2010 fails it, which is why league-wide RAPM starts
in 2011. The card reports between about 76% and 80% of possessions usable in
the early seasons.

## How the model works

Each possession is one row of a regression. Each player has an offensive column
and a defensive column, switched on when she is on the court for that side. The
model also has an intercept (the league's average points per 100 possessions)
and a home-court term. The outcome is the points scored.

Ordinary least squares would fail: players who share most of their minutes are
nearly impossible to separate, and players with a handful of possessions would
get wild estimates. Ridge regression adds a penalty on the size of every
coefficient, which shrinks players toward zero (league average) unless the data
pull them away:

$$
\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \; \sum_i w_i (y_i - x_i^\top \beta)^2 + \lambda \lVert \beta \rVert^2
$$

As reported in the model card, the league-wide fit uses $\lambda = 1000$, fixed by
a validation program and checked at run time so a silently unregularized fit
cannot publish. The card reports intercepts between about 87 and 93 points per
100 possessions and home-court advantage between about 2.4 and 2.8 points per
100 across seasons, and uses both as scale checks: a normalization bug moves
them out of band even when the player ordering survives.

Shrinkage is visible in the published ratings: the fewer possessions a player
has, the closer her estimate sits to zero.

```{r shrinkage, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of 2025-26 NCAA women's league-wide RAPM magnitude against offensive possessions; low-possession players cluster near zero."}
ggplot(rapm, aes(off_poss, abs(rapm_net))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, color = "#221A4D") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "#b298dc", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(
    title = "Shrinkage: low-possession players are pulled toward zero",
    x = "Offensive possessions", y = "|RAPM| (points per 100)",
    caption = "Data: wehoop::load_ncaa_wbb_rapm(seasons = 2026)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Uncertainty

The model card describes ridge posterior standard errors for every player
(`orapm_se`, `drapm_se`, `rapm_net_se`) and a split-half calibration check:
the season's games are split in two, both halves are refit, and each player's
two estimates are compared with the standard errors. As reported in the card,
the published (posterior) standard errors are conservative by about 2.5 times
relative to how much an estimate moves between two halves of a season, and a
typical player's standard error is about 4 points per 100. The card's advice:
read `rapm_net` plus or minus two standard errors as a cautious band, and treat
overlapping bands as a tier, not a ranking.

```{r se-columns}
intersect(c("orapm_se", "drapm_se", "rapm_net_se"), names(rapm))
```

At the time this page was built the release file that `load_ncaa_wbb_rapm()`
reads did not include the standard error columns (the result above is empty when
they are absent). The practical point stands either way: at roughly 4 points per
100 of uncertainty, the top of any RAPM leaderboard is a group of players, not an
order.

## Within-team RAPM

Within-team RAPM fits each team separately. It answers "who drives this team's
results" rather than "who is best in the country".

```{r within}
within <- load_ncaa_wbb_rapm_within_team(seasons = 2026)

within |>
  filter(team == "UConn") |>
  arrange(desc(rapm_net)) |>
  select(team, player_code, rapm_off, rapm_def, rapm_net, team_off_poss, num_players) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  head(8)
```

**Mind the defensive sign.** The two files use different conventions. In the
league-wide file a positive `drapm` is good and `rapm_net = orapm + drapm`. In
the within-team file `rapm_def` is measured in points allowed, so a **negative**
value is good and `rapm_net = rapm_off - rapm_def`. Check it on the data before
combining them:

```{r sign-check}
c(
  league_net_is_o_plus_d = isTRUE(all.equal(rapm$rapm_net, rapm$orapm + rapm$drapm,
                                            tolerance = 1e-6)),
  within_net_is_o_minus_d = isTRUE(all.equal(within$rapm_net, within$rapm_off - within$rapm_def,
                                             tolerance = 1e-6))
)
```

Comparing the two net estimates for the same players:

```{r compare-estimands}
stopifnot(identical(class(rapm$player_id), class(within$player_id)))

both <- inner_join(
  rapm |> select(player_id, league_net = rapm_net, off_poss, def_poss),
  within |> select(player_id, within_net = rapm_net),
  by = "player_id"
)

both |>
  filter(off_poss + def_poss >= 800) |>
  summarise(players = n(), correlation = cor(league_net, within_net))
```

They agree broadly but not exactly. A player on a deep team shares credit with
good teammates in the within-team fit, while the league-wide fit also credits her
for how her team performs against the rest of Division I. Use within-team RAPM to
compare teammates, and league-wide RAPM for everything else.

## How well does it work?

As reported in the model card, the league-wide model is gated before publishing
on every season:

- the usable-possession share must be at least 0.65;
- the intercept must sit in an 83 to 98 band, and home-court advantage in a
  1 to 4 band, per 100 possessions;
- the standard error checks must pass (standard errors fall as possessions rise,
  and the split-half calibration coverage stays in band).

Externally, a team's possession-weighted average of its players' RAPM is
compared with Bart Torvik's adjusted efficiency margin. As reported in the card,
the rank correlation (Spearman) is about 0.98 for 2023 through 2026 and 0.90 for
2021; Torvik has no women's ratings before 2021, so earlier seasons carry no
external check. This validates the **team-level** aggregate, not the ordering of
individual players.

## Fit your own WNBA RAPM with `wnba_rapm()` {#fit-your-own-wnba-rapm-with-wnba_rapm}

`wehoop` exports a ridge RAPM you can run yourself. `wnba_rapm()` takes any
possession table with `off_player_1` to `off_player_5`, `def_player_1` to
`def_player_5` (player ids) and `points`, and returns one row per player with
`o_rapm`, `d_rapm`, `rapm`, `off_poss` and `def_poss`. Under the hood it:

- builds a sparse design with one offensive and one defensive indicator column
  per player, dropping possessions with an incomplete lineup;
- fits a ridge regression with `glmnet` and an unpenalized intercept (so the
  ratings are relative to average), choosing the penalty by
  10-fold cross-validation with fixed, deterministic folds, so repeated calls
  give identical results without setting a seed;
- multiplies by 100 and flips the sign of the defensive coefficient so that good
  defense is positive.

It needs the `glmnet` and `Matrix` packages. The function's documentation notes
that a full season of possessions is needed for stable estimates; a single game
is for illustration only.

`load_wnba_stats_possessions()` publishes WNBA possessions with lineups from a
GitHub release, so a full season fits in seconds without calling the WNBA Stats
API:

```{r wnba-rapm}
poss <- load_wnba_stats_possessions(seasons = 2025) |>
  # regular-season WNBA Stats game ids start with "102"
  filter(substr(game_id, 1, 3) == "102", count_as_possession == TRUE)

nrow(poss)

my_rapm <- wnba_rapm(poss)

nrow(my_rapm)
```

How close is this to the published suite, which uses its own penalty and
design? Compare with the regular-season RAPM in `load_wnba_player_impact()`:

```{r wnba-compare}
published <- load_wnba_player_impact(seasons = 2025) |>
  filter(season_type == "Regular Season") |>
  select(player_id, player_name, pub_rapm = rapm, pub_o = o_rapm, pub_d = d_rapm)

stopifnot(identical(class(my_rapm$player_id), class(published$player_id)))

compare <- inner_join(my_rapm, published, by = "player_id") |>
  filter(off_poss >= 1000)

compare |>
  summarise(
    players = n(),
    r_offense = cor(o_rapm, pub_o),
    r_defense = cor(d_rapm, pub_d),
    r_total = cor(rapm, pub_rapm),
    sd_wnba_rapm = sd(rapm),
    sd_published = sd(pub_rapm)
  )
```

```{r wnba-compare-plot, fig.alt = "Scatter plot comparing RAPM fitted with wnba_rapm() against the published WNBA player impact RAPM for 2025 players with at least 1,000 offensive possessions."}
ggplot(compare, aes(pub_rapm, rapm)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, color = "#221A4D") +
  labs(
    title = "2025 WNBA: wnba_rapm() vs the published suite",
    subtitle = "Players with 1,000+ offensive possessions",
    x = "Published RAPM (load_wnba_player_impact)", y = "wnba_rapm()",
    caption = "Data: wehoop::load_wnba_stats_possessions(), wehoop::load_wnba_player_impact()"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

For regular-rotation players the two rank players very similarly. Compare the
two standard deviations above for the difference in spread: the
cross-validated penalty in `wnba_rapm()` is chosen per fit, while the suite uses
its own settings, and a stronger penalty pulls every estimate closer to zero.

To build possessions for a single game yourself, `wnba_possession_lineups()`
calls the WNBA Stats API play-by-play (with on-court players) and returns the same
possession layout. It is a live call to stats.wnba.com, so it is not run here.

```{r one-game, eval = FALSE}
one_game <- wnba_possession_lineups(game_id = "1022500001")
wnba_rapm(one_game)   # illustration only: one game is far too small
```

## Limitations

- **Shrinkage is a choice.** Low-possession players sit near zero because the
  model knows little about them, not because they are average. Filter on
  possessions before ranking.
- **Collinearity.** Players who share nearly all their minutes cannot be
  separated by the data; the penalty decides how their joint effect is split.
- **Team-level validation only.** The external check against Torvik validates the
  team aggregate. There is no public benchmark for individual women's college
  RAPM.
- **Within-team RAPM is not comparable across teams**, and as reported in the
  card it is produced by a manual step that needs the raw play-by-play bundles.
- **Not yet in the published model**, as reported in the card: multi-season
  pooling and a box score prior, both measured in development, and a luck
  adjustment for three-point shooting.
